AI is changing the economics and speed of cyberattacks. In September 2026, The Wall Street Journal reported that a three-person security research team used Anthropic’s Claude to chain together software flaws and reach OpenAI’s internal code systems. The researchers were white-hat testers working through a bug-bounty program, and the full path from a newly found bug to access took under three days. The lesson is sobering: work that once required a well-resourced team can increasingly be done by a few people using off-the-shelf AI. item.title: 🟠 More control, fewer dependencies: Why DORA is forcing a connectivity rethink
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

If a bank spread its investments across several funds, only to find they were all heavily exposed to the same company, its risk team would have some difficult questions to answer. I think it’s high time CIOs brought that same level of curiosity and skepticism to their network architecture. When we distribute applications across different providers, we need to know where their apparent “independence” actually ends.

Resilience depends on independence. That is, a plan B only works if it isn’t exposed to the same set of variables as Plan A. While a second cloud might open up more options to businesses, its value as a fallback depends entirely on whether people can still reach it if something fails. If the path to both clouds passes through the same infrastructure, a single disruption can leave customers stranded while the applications themselves keep running. That lack of business continuity is a difficult thing for a CIO and their team to explain to the board, particularly when the company has invested so much in resilience, and it’s why I believe that connectivity deserves a seat at the top table.

item.title: 🔵 Claude, Copilot and Agentforce are ready. Are your SAP and ServiceNow platforms ready?
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

At a 2027 planning session in October, I watched a leadership team approve three AI agent pilots in under ten minutes. The three were a claims-intake agent, a collections agent and a finance close assistant, each with a sponsor, a vendor quote and a slide of projected savings. The next item on the agenda was the SAP clean-core program those same agents would run on. It took forty minutes, drew questions about payback and slipped to 2028.

Nobody in the room did anything wrong. The agents came in as an operating expense from the innovation fund and were judged on speed to value. The clean-core program came in as a capital project and was judged on a three-year payback—two committees, two tests, one dependency that neither test could see. The agents were funded. The platform they would run on was not.

Versions of that meeting play out in most of the programs I advise, from banks to state Medicaid agencies. It is the planning mistake I see most often this budget season, and you can fix it before January.

At the TechEd developer conference in Berlin, SAP presented additional details of its “Autonomous Enterprise” concept, which includes AI capabilities via Joule Work and SAP Autonomous Suite, built on the SAP Business AI Platform. The company’s focus is not just AI, but AI agents capable of acting automatically within the SAP system by performing analyses and answering queries.

Nginx, the web server estimated to power a third of the internet, has shipped fixes for multiple vulnerabilities, including a critical unauthenticated remote code execution flaw that puts millions of websites at risk and has existed in the code for over a decade. Researchers from several security firms independently found some of the same flaws by using AI agents, adding to a string of recent AI-discovered vulnerabilities in widely used internet technologies such as PHP, Node, OpenSSH, and Java.

The most severe flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-123007, lets an attacker manipulate flow-control windows in the HTTP/2 protocol implementation to trigger an out-of-bounds memory copy that researchers from Xint.io turned into command execution with Nginx worker privileges. The vulnerability affects every official Nginx release for more than 10 years since version 1.9.5, which originally added HTTP/2 support in 2015.
